title: Real Vector Spaces (4.1)
description: True/false questions on the 8 vector space axioms, including several classic 'is this actually a vector space' traps. 8 questions pulled per attempt from a pool of 25.

questions.prompt: A vector space's zero vector must be unique.
explanations: If 0 and 0' were both zero vectors, then 0 = 0 + 0' = 0' + 0 = 0' — so there can only be one.

questions.prompt: If a set is closed under both addition and scalar multiplication, it is automatically a vector space.
explanations: Closure is necessary but not sufficient. You also need commutativity, associativity, a zero vector, additive inverses, the unit property, and both distributive laws to all hold.

questions.prompt: The scalars used in a vector space must always be real numbers.
explanations: Scalars can come from other fields too — for example ℂⁿ is a vector space over the complex numbers, using complex scalars.

questions.prompt: V = ℝ with u⊕v := max(u,v) (and ordinary scalar multiplication) fails to be a vector space because it has no zero vector.
explanations: You'd need a single e with max(u,e)=u for every real u, but u is unbounded below, so no fixed e works for all u.

questions.prompt: V = ℝ³ with ordinary scalar multiplication but u⊕v := (u1+v1, u2+v2, 0) is a vector space, since addition here is still commutative and associative.
explanations: Commutative and associative, yes — but there's still no zero vector. You'd need e3=0 to satisfy u3+e3=u3 for EVERY u3, and u3 ranges over all of ℝ.

questions.prompt: In a vector space, 0·v = 0 for every vector v (the scalar zero times any vector gives the zero vector).
explanations: This is provable from the 8 axioms: 0v = (0+0)v = 0v+0v, so adding -(0v) to both sides gives 0 = 0v.

questions.prompt: If k·v = 0 for a scalar k and vector v, then k must be 0.
explanations: It's also possible that v = 0 itself (with k ≠ 0), since k·0 = 0 for any scalar k. The correct rule is k·v = 0 implies k=0 OR v=0.

questions.prompt: Treating points on the unit circle as angles, with addition = adding angles and scalar multiplication = scaling angles (both reduced mod 2π), gives a valid vector space.
explanations: Scalar multiplication isn't associative here: (km)θ ≠ k(mθ) once you reduce mod 2π. Example: θ=π, m=2, k=½ gives k(mθ) = ½·0 = 0, but (km)θ = 1·π = π.

questions.prompt: V = ℝ with ordinary addition but scalar multiplication redefined as k·x := 0 for every k and x fails to be a vector space because the unit property (1·x = x) fails.
explanations: 1·x = 0 for every x here, but the unit property requires 1·x = x — so it fails for every x ≠ 0. (Every other axiom happens to still hold, some only trivially.)

questions.prompt: The set of all finite lists of real numbers, with addition defined as list concatenation, is commutative.
explanations: [1,2]+[3] = [1,2,3], but [3]+[1,2] = [3,1,2] — different lists, so order matters and addition is not commutative.

questions.prompt: If you fix the commutativity problem above by sorting the concatenated list, the result is a valid vector space.
explanations: Sorting does fix commutativity, but concatenation only ever makes a list longer — so no nonzero list has an additive inverse that concatenates it back down to the empty list.

questions.prompt: Every vector space must contain infinitely many vectors.
explanations: The trivial vector space {0}, containing only the zero vector, satisfies all 8 axioms with just one element.

questions.prompt: In any vector space, the additive inverse -v is always equal to (-1)·v.
explanations: This follows from the 8 axioms: v + (-1)v = 1v + (-1)v = (1+(-1))v = 0v = 0, so (-1)v really is v's additive inverse.

questions.prompt: The set of 2×2 matrices, with ordinary matrix addition and scalar multiplication, forms a vector space.
explanations: Matrix addition and scalar multiplication satisfy all 8 axioms — the zero matrix is the identity, and -A is the inverse of A.

questions.prompt: V = ℝ with u⊕v := (u+v)/2 (the average of u and v) and ordinary scalar multiplication is a vector space, since averaging two reals is commutative.
explanations: Commutative, yes, but there's no zero vector: (u+0)/2 = u/2 ≠ u unless u=0, and no other fixed candidate works for every u either.

questions.prompt: In any vector space, if u + w = v + w, then u = v.
explanations: This is the cancellation law. Add -w (which exists by axiom 4) to both sides: (u+w)+(-w) = (v+w)+(-w), which simplifies to u = v.

questions.prompt: A vector space must have some 'multiplication' operation between two vectors, like a dot product.
explanations: The 8 axioms only involve vector addition and scalar-times-vector multiplication. A vector-times-vector product isn't part of the definition at all.

questions.prompt: The set of real-valued functions defined on an interval, with the usual pointwise addition and scalar multiplication of functions, is a vector space.
explanations: Pointwise addition and scaling of functions satisfy all 8 axioms — the zero function is the identity, and (-f) is the inverse of f.

questions.prompt: If a candidate structure satisfies 7 of the 8 axioms, it can still be called a vector space as long as most of the axioms hold.
explanations: All 8 axioms are required, with no partial credit — failing even one (like the unit property in the k·x=0 example) disqualifies the structure entirely.

questions.prompt: The empty set (with no elements at all) can be a valid vector space.
explanations: Every vector space must contain at least the zero vector, by the existence-of-zero-vector axiom — so it can never be empty.

questions.prompt: Two very different-looking structures — say, polynomials and 2x2 matrices — can both be genuine vector spaces.
explanations: The 8 axioms only care about how addition and scalar multiplication behave, not what the objects literally are — polynomials, matrices, and functions can all be 'vectors'.

questions.prompt: If associativity of addition fails for a structure, then a zero vector can never exist for that structure either.
explanations: These are independent axioms. The u⊕v=max(u,v) example is actually associative and STILL has no zero vector — failing one axiom doesn't force another one to fail too.

questions.prompt: Every vector space over the real numbers automatically satisfies (k+m)v = kv + mv for all scalars k, m and every vector v.
explanations: This is one of the 8 axioms itself (distributivity of scalar multiplication over scalar addition) — it holds by definition, not something extra to check.

questions.prompt: The set of all polynomials of degree EXACTLY 2 (not less), with the usual addition, is a vector space.
explanations: It fails closure: (x²+x) + (-x²+1) = x+1, which has degree 1, not exactly 2 — the sum leaves the set. (Degree ≤ 2, by contrast, IS closed and IS a vector space.)

questions.prompt: If a structure fails only the unit property (1·v = v) but satisfies every other axiom, it is still not a vector space.
explanations: All 8 axioms are required simultaneously, with no exception for the unit property — this is exactly what happens in the k·x=0 example.
